question: Meesho Data Scientist-1, Round 3 (ML breadth, case study). **How would you build a visual search system for Meesho?** The interviewer focused on model building: **explain how a Vision Transformer (ViT) works, which model you would select and why, how you would train it, and which evaluation and business metrics you would track.**
lookingFor: Can you frame the problem (retrieval, embeddings, ranking) and state requirements?
Do you pick a reasonable model and training objective with justification?
Do you consider data, labels and negatives, and serving at scale?
Do you pair offline retrieval metrics with online business metrics?
Do you anticipate failure modes (domain shift, near duplicates, cold start)?
answer:
**Problem framing.** A shopper uploads or taps a photo and gets visually similar (or the same) products from a large catalogue of images. This is **image retrieval**: map every image to an embedding, then do nearest-neighbour search. Clarify latency (for example a few hundred milliseconds), catalogue size, whether exact-match and similar-style both matter, and cold start for new products.

**How ViT works.** Split the image into fixed patches (for example 16x16), flatten and linearly project each to a token, add positional embeddings and a class token, then pass through standard transformer encoder layers (self-attention plus MLP). The class token or pooled output is the image representation. ViT lacks CNN inductive biases, so it needs large-scale pretraining but then scales well and captures global context.

**Model choice.** Start from a **pretrained backbone**, either a ViT or a CNN such as ResNet/EfficientNet, ideally a CLIP-style or self-supervised model (such as DINO) that gives strong general features. Trade-off: ViT gives better quality; a smaller CNN or distilled model gives lower latency and cost. Baseline first: pretrained embeddings with no fine-tuning.

**Training.** Fine-tune with **metric learning**: contrastive or triplet loss so that images of the same product (different photos, user photos vs catalogue shots) are close and different products are far, with hard-negative mining. Positives come from multiple images of one product, augmentations and click/purchase pairs from logs. Add category or attribute heads as auxiliary tasks. Use cropping or detection to isolate the item from the background.

**Serving.** Compute embeddings offline for the catalogue, store them in an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, IVF-PQ), embed the query at request time, retrieve top-K, then re-rank using category, price, availability and personalisation.

**Evaluation.** Offline: recall@K, precision@K, mAP, NDCG on a labelled query set, sliced by category. Online: A/B test on click-through rate, add-to-cart, conversion, search abandonment, plus latency and revenue per session.

**Risks.** Domain gap between user photos and studio images, near-duplicate listings, index drift as catalogue changes, bias towards popular items.
followUps: Why use contrastive or triplet loss instead of classification?
How do you mine hard negatives?
How would you evaluate if there is no labelled relevance data?
How would you handle new products added every hour?
ViT vs CNN: when would you choose each?
